subsubtopic: JUDGE OF THE EXCHEQUER COURT OF CANADA
speechtext:
Before the bill is read a second time I should like to suggest that we should have what in some legislatures is known as a legal committee. A great many members of the House of Commons are not lawyers, and it may be a good thing that they are not, but I believe this house needs a committee on legal bills of this kind. Five or six matters have arisen, of which this bill is one, to which a legal committee could usefully give consideration-matters affecting the judges, their status, the question of salaries, criminal code amendment, the justice department, and related legal subjects. I believe that such a committee would strengthen the hands of the Attorney General of Canada, the present Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent). He is right most of the time, and I hope that shortly he will be promoted and become right honourable, perhaps when the birthday honours are announced.
Another matter for such a committee was referred to several times by Chief Justice Robertson in the Ontario court of appeal, namely the problem of delinquency. I hope the minister will consider this suggestion for such bill as the one now before us. I support the second reading of the bill.
Mr. A. II. BENCE (Saskatoon City): This bill gives us an opportunity of drawing one or two matters to the attention of the administration with respect to the judiciary. The position which the judiciary of this country finds itself in at the present time should, I believe, be broadly reviewed for the purpose of determining whether the conditions which exist are the best possible in the interests of the administration of justice. There are a number of important questions which must be given serious consideration. One of the first is, are we providing sufficient compensation for the judiciary to attract the very best type of man to the bench? It seems to me, in view of the fact that the judges are the custodians of the rights of the people, and sit in judgment on matters which concern the liberty and the property of the subject, they should be in a position, financially and otherwise, so that no question might arise about their being beyond reproach. It is not asking too much of parliament to suggest that the scale of financial remuneration of the judges be such that, first of all, we can obtain the
best men available, and, second, that once they have been placed in the judicial position, they shall have no undue worries as far as their financial future is concerned.
In connection with this matter I would draw to the attention of the minister and the administration a matter which I know has created considerable concern among members of the legal fraternity, namely the fact that no provision is made for the maintenance of widows and dependents of deceased judges.
I should also like to take this opportunity of discussing the vexed question of the compulsory retirement, of judges. This matter has been referred to on a number of occasions, not only in this house but in the press. The situation which exists with respect to compulsory retirement is, to say the least, anomalous. Under the provisions of the British North America Act the governor general, which is to say the government, is authorized to appoint two different types of judges, those of the county or district court, and those of the superior court of the province, consisting of the trial judges and the appellate judges. In addition to that, under the provisions of the other acts which are in existence, the Supreme Court Act and the Exchequer Court Act, the governor general may also appoint judges to the supreme court and to the exchequer court.
With respect to judges of the district or county courts, the lowest courts to which appointments are made by the government, there is a provision that there shall be compulsory retirement at the age of seventy-five. That provision is contained in the Judges Act, and I believe was first passed in 1913.
The provisions for the supreme court are contained in the Supreme Court Act, and we find that the justices of that court are also compulsorily retired at the age of seventy-five years. That provision came in a little later, and was passed by parliament in 1927. Section 9 of the Supreme Court Act states:
9. The judges shall hold office during good behaviour, but shall be removable by the governor general on address of the Senate and House of Commons: Provided that each judge, whether heretofore appointed or hereafter to be appointed, shall cease to hold office upon attaining the age of seventy-five years, or immediately, if he has already attained that age.
A similar provision was placed in the Exchequer Court Act at that time. Thus we now find ourselves in the position where judges of the lower courts, namely the county or district courts, and judges of the highest court of the land, namely the Supreme Court of Canada, are compulsorily retired at the age of seventy-five years. On the other hand, members of what I might describe as the intermediate court, referred to as the superior
Judges Act

court, consisting of the trial and appellate courts, are not subject to the same provision. We find ourselves in the position where we have men sitting on those courts who have attained ages as great as ninety years. We have had many examples of judges over eighty years of age who have sat in these courts.
I believe I should first point out the reason for this condition. District court, county jourt and supreme court judges are appointed rnder acts of parliament, and hold office by virtue of those acts. On the other hand, superior court judges hold office partly by virtue of a provision contained in the British North America Act, to be found in volume 5 of the Revised Statutes of Canada. Section 99 of that act states:
99. The judges of the superior courts shall hold office during good behaviour, but shall foe removable foy the governor general on address of the Senate and House of Commons.
Consequently, as a result of the provisions of that act, parliament has no authority to deal with the compulsory retirement of judges of the superior court. On the other hand, parliament has authority to deal with, and has dealt with judges of other courts.
As I said before, the provisions respecting the compulsory retirement of supreme court judges were brought into effect in 1927, at which time considerable discussion took place in the house. It was decided at that time that there should be compulsory retirement, and that it should be retroactive.
The next step in the picture came in 1933, at which time a measure was introduced and passed in the house, despite the opposition of hon. members of the party now occupying the treasury benches. The measure at that time did not deal with compulsory retirement, but provided that when a judge of the superior court reached the age of seventy-five his salary would be reduced to the amount of the pension he would receive if then retired. In my opinion the method adopted to achieve the purpose the administration had in mind was not the best one available. In other words, it was a roundabout way of achieving an object which, I believe, could have been attained in a direct fashion.
At the time that matter was before the house for consideration a fairly lengthy debate took place. The objection taken to the measure was voiced briefly by the then leader of the opposition, the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), when he stated, as reported at page 4790 of Hansard for 1932-33:
The provisions of this bill appear to violate contracts between the crown and members of the judiciary. Perhaps my hon. friend would explain to us on the second reading whether that is the case or not, and if it is the case, on what grounds he justifies the measure at all.

Subsequently, during the debate, the Right Hon, Mr. Lapointe took strenuous objection to the effect that the legislation would be a breach of contract between the judges and the crown. Generally speaking, it was opposed on that basis by members of the Liberal party then sitting in opposition. It is indicated in Mr. Lapointe's speech that they felt the question of politics came into the consideration of the administration, and he [DOT]pointed out the following at page 4795 of Hansard for the same year:
I am free to confess that I believe the purpose is to create vacancies for the appointment of new judges.
Unfortunately, I believe one of the greatest difficulties different administrations in this country have encountered has been that oppositions have felt that the reason why certain measures were being introduced might be partly political, giving the administration of the day an opportunity to fill appointments from adherents of their own political groups. It seems to me that was a great mistake. Surely the attitude taken at that time was the wrong one, because if the measure had been passed by parliament we would not find ourselves in the impossible position we have to-day, and the situation would have been immeasurably improved by this time. Possibly I should add in passing that while the measure was passed by the House of Commons, it was eventually turned down by the senate on the grounds advanced by the then opposition in the house.
I am not in favour of a policy of breaking contractual obligations with anyone, certainly least of all the judges. I believe this problem could have been solved quite easily in another way. First of all, an amendment should be made to the British North America Act so that parliament could deal with superior court judges in the same way as it deals with judges of the lower courts, and with those of the highest court in the land. There would appear to be no sound reason whatsoever why that should not be done. A provision could be inserted in the proper act along the same line as those provisions now applicable to other judges, and there could be compulsory retirement at the age of seventy-five.
In order, however, that there may be no question of breach of contract, I believe it should be provided that the compulsory retirement would not apply to present members of the judiciary, or that financial provisions be made whereby those now sitting in the various courts might be compulsorily retired at seventy-five, but with the full salary they now receive. In that way we would avoid

Judges Act
being accused of a breach of faith which otherwise might follow. It would only be a few years before the matter would be completely straightened out. Judges now on the bench could be permitted to act until they retired or were possibly removed, a procedure that is not often adopted in this country, and then provision could be made with respect to new appointees on the same basis as now applies to the district courts and the Supreme Court of Canada. In accepting an appointment, a man would know exactly what his position was. If it is felt that something should be done immediately about the retirement of judges who have reached seventy-five years of age, I think we should consider giving compensation on the basis of their present income. That is the only fair and sensible solution of the problem.
I do not want to get into any argument as to whether any particular man who is over seventy-five years of age still retains his faculties sufficiently to perform his duties in the same manner as he did in earlier life, because there are certain exceptional examples of men who can do this. However, I think generally speaking it must be concluded that when a man has reached seventy-five years of age his faculties are not nearly as good as they were when he was younger. In addition, I believe the public has not as much confidence in the judgment and ability of a man of eighty-five or ninety years of age as in the judgment and ability of men twenty or twenty-five years younger. We must consider the position of the public in this matter, because the administration of justice affects the public. These courts have been created and these judges have been appointed purely and simply for the purpose of being of service to the public. Also, if judges were retired greater opportunity would be given to younger and more aggressive men to enter the judicial field.
I think the political angle should be entirely disregarded. I doubt if there will be any opposition, or at least not very much, from any of the parties in this house should the administration decide to proceed along the lines I have suggested. I do not think it will be contended that vacancies were being created for the purpose of appointing particular men.
This matter has to be faced, and the sooner it is faced the better. When the exchequer court bill was before the house I took the stand that judicial appointments should be made as quickly as possible. The minister took exception to my remarks and suggested that I had said that such appointments were dangled before the eyes of prospective
appointees. I was not making that suggestion with respect to the minister himself; I was making it with respect to the administration generally. I think it is agreed that in many cases appointments are held up because of the political situation in which certain gentlemen find themselves. That is a situation which should be avoided if at all possible. The minister may think the administration of justice in Saskatchewan has not been impaired because a certain position has not been filled, but in the long run I think it is a better policy not to put off these appointments indefinitely. The minister will clear up this matter to my satisfaction, and I am sure to the satisfaction of all members of this house, if he makes this appointment to the vacancy which exists there as soon as possible and not let politics intervene in any way. The minister has referred to the fact that members of the legal fraternity who were not adherents of the political party at present in power have been appointed to the bench by this government. He may know of such cases, but I must say they have not come to my attention and I do not think they exist in Saskatchewan. I suggest to the minister that the present vacancy in that province offers an admirable opportunity to him to demonstrate the spirit which he has suggested exists. Possibly some leading member of the Progressive Conservative party could be appointed to that post.
As far as the situation in that province is concerned I should like to reiterate emphatically a protest which I made when the exchequer court bill was before us. I believe we have reached a time when the learned gentleman who occupies a high post in the diplomatic service of this country as high commissioner to Australia should make up his mind, or the administration should make up his mind, either to continue in the diplomatic service or to return to his duties on the bench. Personally I think it is unfair that he should be allowed to retain a judgeship in his hip-pocket, so to speak, while he spends a number of years in other countries.

speakeroldname: Mr. S. H. KNOWLES (Winnipeg North Centre):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take just a few minutes to express my support of the contention of the previous speaker that steps should be taken as early as possible to strengthen the position of the judiciary in the eyes of the people of this country. I feel he has done something worth while in the presentation he has made in connection with the desirability of the retirement of judges of the provincial superior courts at a determined age. As he has pointed out, we find ourselves in a rather odd position. The judges of our highest courts, the Supreme
Judges Act

Court of Canada and the Exchequer Court of Canada, and those of the lower courts are subject to compulsory retirement. On the other hand, judges of courts in the so-called middle brackets, the provincial superior courts, are appointed for life. The British North America Act denies either to this parliament or to the provincial legislatures the right to fix a compulsory retiring age for these judges.
While it is agreed that some men of ripe years maintain their mental and physical vigour, I think as a general rule it would be much better for the administration of justice and the prestige of our courts if we adopted the principle that the judges in all courts should retire at a fixed age. In my view the retiring age of seventy-five years which applies to those judges who are compelled to retire, and which is the age the hon. member for Saskatoon City (Mr. Bence) thinks should be applied in all cases, is too high. I believe in this day a lower age should be fixed and I suggest that seventy years might be given consideration. When I use the phrase "might be given consideration" I do so in the hope that the government is giving serious thought to this matter. I dare to hope that when the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) speaks, as I hope he will a little later on, he will give some indication whether this matter is under consideration by the government.
In the province from which I come, one of the newspapers on its editorial page not long ago gave itself to an expression of opinion on this whole question. I think many of us will agree it was regrettable that the kind of thing had to be said that was contained in that particular editorial. The principal objection was that it seemed by inference to cast reflection on some of the older men of one of the courts of Manitoba who undoubtedly had given good service. It is not necessary for me to defend the Winnipeg Free Press, but I do wish to say it is regrettable that that kind of situation could develop where, in order to press an important point such as this it seemed necessary to involve the prestige and personalities of revered gentlemen such as those who have sat on our bench. That, of course, was not intended, but it grew out of the failure of governments of the past, as well as the present administration, to deal with this matter.
I feel that the previous speaker is on sound ground when he suggests that we should not delay further in connection with this matter. I understand that at the present time in the provincial superior courts of the country- these courts have a wide range of names- there are twenty-nine judges between the

ages of seventy and seventy-five, and eleven judges of the age of seventy-six or over, running as high as ninety-two years.
Like the previous speaker, I affirm that undoubtedly there are men in the higher brackets with mental and physical vigour greater than that of many who are much younger, but as a general principle I think members of this house will be agreed that there ought to be fixed a reasonable retiring age for judges of all courts in this country. I agree with the previous speaker in his suggestion that an amendment to the British North America Act should be sought to make this possible. If there are reasons which make it difficult to secure such an amendment for a period of time, I would suggest that some other method might be found to bring about this result. I have, as a matter of fact, on the order paper a bill which, while not in a sense concerned with the retirement of judges, would have that effect. My purpose in rising at this time is to express the hope that during the course of this debate the Minister of Justice will give us some indication as to whether or not the retirement of judges of the provincial superior courts is being given consideration.
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice): Mr. Speaker, I think in about two minutes I can give the assurance that hon. members have sought, that at the very first opportunity the matter of an amendment to the British North America Act to deal with the provision which now gives judges of the provincial superior courts a life tenure in their office will be considered. This is in my opinion a matter which should not be presented for amendment to the imperial parliament without previous discussion with the provinces, because the administration of justice and the establishment of the courts are matters that are within provincial jurisdiction. It is my view that the proper procedure with respect to amendments to the British North America Act when dealing with any portion that gives jurisdiction to provincial legislatures should involve prior conference and consultation with the legislatures, and if it is sought to take away from them something which has been allotted to them, their consent should be obtained.

Mr. ST. It is a matter which was on the agenda for discussion at the last provincial conference, and it certainly will be one of the matters to be considered at the next provincial conference. All I can say to the house is that as far as I am concerned I would recommend that that conference agree to an amendment to the constitution to give the proper Canadian authorities the right to fix an age limit for the exercise of judicial authority. I am not going to discuss at the present time whether it should be seventy or seventy-five years. I think that is a matter which should be left entirely to the good judgment of the Canadian legislatures including this dominion house, and I would hope that the provincial legislatures would find it in the general interest to leave that to the discretion of parliament, as it is in the discretion of parliament with respect to federal courts and with respect to district and county courts.
As, however, everyone here has recognized, the direct way of going about it will be to get an amendment to the British North America Act, and then have parliament deal with it in its wisdom, as it should be dealt with according to the circumstances.
For the supreme court and the exchequer court-and of course this -bill is only concerned with the exchequer court-the age limit -that parliament has seen fit to set is seventy-five, and the 'same age limit has been set for the district and county courts. I do not think the constitution should fix what -the age limit should be. I think it should be left entirely to the Canadian legislatures to determine from time to time what the proper age limit should be. At least one member of our group desires to say something on this this item.

I shall not be long. Unfortunately, I had to be out of the house during the time much of the debate was carried on. I was in when the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) spoke, and I congratulate him upon the presentation he made and upon the clear evidence of how he digs into matters in which he is interested. He presented an exhaustive statement to the committee. I was in when the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) spoke. I greatly enjoyed his speech, too, because of the amount of material he presented. Many of the other hon. members made excellent speeches as well, but I do not recall them at the moment. The two committees of which I am a member took up a good deal of my time and therefore I missed much of the debate. I was in last evening when the minister spoke and I enjoyed his remarks. He was much more explicit last night than he was when I heard him on March 17. If he had said on March 17 what he said last evening, perhaps the debate would have been shortened. However, I feel I ought to state my position as clearly and as briefly as I can.
I am convinced that the discussion so far has done good and that much information has come out. I keep asking myself, as I did in the beginning, when I heard the minister speak on March 17, what is the situation? I say frankly I was greatly dismayed. Not knowing all the facts at that time I feared the direction in which we were headed. I have always been a strong advocate of maintaining Canada's sovereignty in full. For years I have looked forward to a great expansion in Canada's airway programme. I envisioned some city in the maritimes being made the centre of air operations in that section. I am not familiar enough with the airfields in the maritimes, or the air currents,

War Appropriation-Transport
fogs and so forth that would have to be taken into consideration in the establishment of airfields, to know much about the best centre there; but I presume some one big centre could be developed from which Canada's whole eastern air programme would be operated.
I had envisioned Montreal as a great air centre. When I speak of Montreal I mean the airfields adjacent to Montreal and used by that city and vicinity. I had envisioned an airfield there from which the whole territory north to Ungava and perhaps Baffin Land, when that territory is opened, as it will be by-and-by, both commercially and for passenger traffic, could be served. I know enough about the north to realize that its resources are far beyond the conception of the average Canadian, in fact beyond the conception of most people anywhere. I have envisaged an air transport service some day, consisting of planes of one to three hundred tons capacity and even more, moving products down to Montreal from the north. I envisage another great airport at or near Toronto. I am not sure whether the department have finally settled on any specific site, although they do use Malton and perhaps the island airfield. Certainly the country north from Toronto around Hudson bay will open up for both commerce and passenger traffic a great field of future expansion. The same applies to the country north of Winnipeg along the west coast of the Hudson bay, in which area minerals are being discovered. I fancy I can see in the future great fleets of aeroplanes coming down from the north, helping to build up Winnipeg into a great city of half a million or more. The same applies to Prince Albert, perhaps the last really big centre for northern Saskatchewan, which has a great northern hinterland. The same is also true of Edmonton. Every time I go into the territory north of Edmonton, whether by boat, plane or otherwise, I picture to myself the day when Edmonton will be a city of half a million. It has, I am convinced, one of the surest futures of any of our cities. The same would apply to Vancouver or whatever airfield is established near that city for traffic on the west coast and across to Asia.
So that I had envisioned a great and wide air programme for Canada, and when I heard the minister speak my heart went down, for, I said to myself, "This is all going to be put, at least to a certain extent, under foreign control." In that I may be wrong; I hope I am. But when I read the minister's speech, and I have read it carefully two or three times, I first asked myself, "Just why the
hurry to submit either to this house or to any other body our proposals?" To come back to the subject of the national airways, has the minister, both in his remarks and in the draft agreement, indicated that we are to have full possession of the air over our respective countries? In the words of article II, section 1:
Each member state recognizes that every state has complete exclusive sovereignty over the air space above its territory.

The authority-
That is the international authority which is to be set up, not the local authority, and on which Canada will presumably have her fair share of members.

To my way of thinking, if an outside international authority has control over air lines in Canada or between Canada and the United States, that is a surrender of our own absolute control over airways in Canada; and it seems to me that, if that is the case, we would always have to submit to some international authority a request to multiply and extend our air lines. I foresee great expansion to the north. Canada's northern territory has not even been scratched. An extremely limited survey of these areas reveals that they are full to overflowing of resources and have vast possibilities. Steffansson, the great arctic explorer, who has written so much about the north, spent a couple of years in the arctic without having taken with him any resources for the maintenance of himself and his crews, in order to demonstrate to the world that the white man can live in the north without supplies from the south. Having made discoveries of vast resources up there, he has recorded them in his books.
I myself, while on my trips to the north, have met many other men who have been farther north than I have, priests and clergymen of the Anglican church and the Roman Catholic church who have lived for many years in Baffin island, Southampton island, Banks island and elsewhere, and all of them record the existence of great resources. The time is coming when Canada will not only receive from our incomparable north vast resources but enjoy the possession of a playground which, even though it be cold for part of the year, will be visited by millions of tourists. In the course of his remarks the minister said that about two years ago he had invited representatives of the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Canadian National Railways and Canadian Airways to sit in and to cooperate under one management. I cannot find anything but praise for either of our two great railway systems because both have done marvellous jobs. Perhaps the Canadian Pacific, being the first in the field, and having been longer in the railway business- although it was not ahead of the old Grand Trunk-deserves unstinted praise and support from this country for the vast contribution it has made to our development. I do not know what Canada would have done had it not been for those wonderful men who built and operated the Canadian Pacific, right down to today. When I say that I am not detracting in any way from the Canadian National system. I am one who greatly admired the work done by the late Sir Henry Thornton. I am one who was deeply sorry when I learned of his sad and tragic end. In my view, even if he made a few mistakes, even if he did take some steps which did not pan out as had been hoped, he deserves great credit.
I am>
convinced that the two big railway companies, either together or separately-and I prefer separately-have done masterly jobs, even if under the minister's direction. The minister did say something about competition. As one who was in big business, one who helped to build big business, I know that the sharpest and strongest competition with which any business house can be confronted is the best possible means of sharpening the wits of the men who are at the head of that business. It induces them to develop their business. I do not believe any big company in Canada would have got anywhere, had it not been for competition.
I am one who believes that competition is the life of trade, and it results in initiative. Why does government service fail? Although occasionally government can do something right, in the great majority of cases businesses operated by governments are failures, because there is no inducement for the management to

that mistake. When this house was told that war was coming, what did we do? The empire is gone unless we have a proper civil aviation policy. When you settle your empire policy you have something to go on in the next step internationally. There is an example of power politics with our ally Russia, and the British are going to make another one with the United States for protection.
In view of these things, how does the policy of the government fit in with the Anglo-Soviet treaty? We do not fit in at all. It is

He stated that medicine is the child of science, the most promising and brightest-eyed of her family. If it has not mastered, it has so diminished as to rob bodily pain of its terrors. Plagues and pestilences have been stayed; a multitude of diseases, diphtheria, rabies, smallpox, typhus, yellow fever, Maltese fever, to mention only a few, were almost exterminated. Great scourge ridden tracts of the earth's surface have been rendered habitable, food values understood, vaccines and anti-toxins discovered, antiseptic surgery so established as to open up new fields of remedial agency, ailments of the mind as well as of the body controlled and relieved. This is a record, indeed, to which no previous age in history can produce a parallel. Within a century the expectation of life in all civilized countries has amazingly increased-in our own by sixteen years; in Denmark by seventeen; in parts of America, by fifteen. Give to man and to his science their due. Who can be blind to such facts or deaf to their eloquence?
That there have been accompanying disadvantages cannot be denied. All goods are associated with evils, and nature will not let us rest. A static world is not, never was and never will be. There have been revolutions in the past, there will be revolutions hereafter, in the world of thought as in the world of events. We must expect the sudden and unpredictable. You may desire a stabilized system, an international agreement to keep things much as they are in respect of national boundaries, and international treaties, material advantages in wealth, air, coal, oil, trade facilities. It will not be given you. For all your entreaties and agreements, the world will not cease to revolve. Nature is no friend of stagnation. Parliaments change; economic conditions change; birth rates rise and fall; labour is cheap here and dear there; a new invention, a new commodity is in demand, and cities spring up to meet it. Factories are built; uninhabited areas become crowded; peoples migrate; once populous districts are deserted. The seats of ancient empires are lost in the desert or the jungle.
We have made practically no discoveries. Take the policy of the government with regard to the Lancaster. My leader is absolutely right about that, and so is Mr. Drew, the premier of Ontario. The Lancaster is not merely a war machine. It can be changed by design, research and equipment. Four to six seats can be placed in it and all that kind of thing. That is where we are, I believe, failing. It is said that the Douglas is more suitable. I read the debate in the British House of Commons on this very question. It was said there

by men who have flown in the air and in all the theatres of war that the Lancaster is a good machine, and could, by research, be fitted .for civil aviation. Their remarks bore out what was said by the gentleman to whom I referred. We are in need of modern research so that we could use the planes to which reference was made.
We are far behind the times. Reference was made to the Boeing plane. Mr. Johnston, once with the Trans-Canada Air Lines, was president. I have nothing against Mr. Symington. He is an old friend of mine and has been since he was at the university of Toronto; but he is on the wrong side of the fence at this time. He has- always been a private ownership man, and one cannot serve two masters at a time like this. That is one of the mistakes that have been made in selecting men for the Trans-Canada Air Lines. That company should be organized from top to bottom and somebody who is a supporter of public ownership put at the head, if we are to have real public ownership. The head is the important man. In the T.C.A. we are getting the same kind of public ownership that we got years ago in the Canadian National Railways between the two wars. I could give the list of companies with which he is associated. I have them here but I shall not refer to them. The whole T.C.A. system should be reorganized from top to bottom and a different man should be at the head.
When our young men come home they will be looking for jobs. You talk about this famous bank, the industrial development bank. That will be a bank to lend money without any security. I am surprised that some of the Scotch members of the committee adopted a policy like that. I am surprised at some of the Scotch members falling for a policy like that, lending money without security, even for feeder lines in civil aviation. I look upon a Scotsman as only an improved Irishman, and I am very much surprised at the Scotch members of the committee adopting such a policy. I read the proceedings of the committee from the point of view of a public ownership man, because I have been an advocate of public ownership and have never deviated from that position.
The present T.C.A. monopoly policy is all wrong. We shall just be putting a lot of yes men in here who will agree to everything the government says about civil aviation, and so far as this phase of their policy on civil aviation is concerned the British empire might just as well disband immediately, if we are to have isolationism and separatism; whereas, by encouraging the empire conference method,
by adopting the aeroplane instead of the cable as a means of commonwealth consultation. We could draw the empire more closely together.

I do not want to make a speech. First, I put this to the minister. This convention is being passed under the provisions of one of the items of the estimates, and included in his statement is the following, as reported in Hansard, page 1580:
Our representatives in the international discussions, therefore, will be authorized to support or initiate such proposals _ as, in the government's opinion, will be likely to result in the establishment of an international air transport authority. . . .
What I wish to know is this: when this matter is concluded and the item is passed, does the minister feel that that is tantamount to an agreement by this House of Commons with respect to the policy set forth in the statement and with respect to the suggested convention, as being matters of policy and as being a matter of a convention with which we as one nation should approach the other nations in the discussion of these proposals? If that is the case, he should take us more completely into his confidence than he has done so far. If we as a House of Commons are expected to pass on these things and come to an agreement upon them, surely we should be taken into his confidence to the extent of knowing as much about it as he does.
Reference was made last evening to the fact that in the latter part of the statement of March 17 there is an allusion to the press statement issued by Lord Beaverbrook at the close of the conference last October. According to Hansard, page 1580, the minister said:
Lord Beaverbrook emphasized the unanimous agreement which the conference had reached on every issue presented to it. He said that those issues were "adequate for testing immediate opinion in relation to civil -aviation."
It seems to me that if we are asked to pass on this thing we should be advised as to what those issues were; they should be set down seriatim, if necessary, so that we can come to a conclusion in our own minds as to what field was canvassed in the discussions and what items were not discussed. In addition, we should be advised as to the attitude which was taken by us and the information

which was obtained by the minister at the conference which he held a short time ago with Mr. Burrell, assistant secretary of state of the United States, prior to Mr. Burrell's departure for England, when he entered into discussions with Lord Beaverbrook. The hon. member for Lake Centre was inquiring last evening of the minister with reference to the matter of an empire set-up, and the most the minister was prepared to say was that there was a discussion of routes between empire countries and that routes between empire countries are wholly consistent with the principles which are laid down in the discussion of international aviation. What I should like to know is whether or not-incidental, if you like, to this discussion which took place in Great Britain last fall-the minister 'considered with the other members of the commonwealth the setting up of an immediate empire system which could be dove-tailed into an international setup; because, as I see it, there may be a great deal of difficulty and it may take a very considerable time to establish an international set-up, whereas we might easily and rapidly come to a conclusion as far as the empire is concerned, and might set up as preliminary to the international organization an empire scheme which would give service within the empire countries. I do not suggest for a minute any scheme which would be opposed to an international arrangement, but it seems to me that grave consideration should be given to this matter I have mentioned, because it is obvious that before we can come to a conclusion on an international scale much time will be occupied and, perhaps, many difficulties encountered.
Lord Beaverbrook, who was one of the leading members of the conference last fall, and has been delegated by the British government to speak on behalf of the government in connection with these deliberations, made reference to the empire in a statement he made last January, which gives an indication that an empire set-up must be in his mind, as incidental to an international set-up, because obviously the international organization was also within his mind if, as was said, the commonwealth had come to conclusion on every issue which had been presented to it, for one of the issues was an international set-up. On January 20, according to the Canadian press, Lord Beaverbrook said:
Our empire can be made to yield to the new science of transportation over the sea and through the air. I hope we shall make good use of our opportunities. We did not in the past.
fMr. Bence.]
From that I conclude he must have had in his mind some kind of empire proposals, possibly along the lines which I have suggested.
The other questions I should like to ask are these: I do not recall that they have been referred to in the discussion so far. First of all, I am curious to find out how it was that the scheme proposed by Canada became public property so long before it was presented to the Canadian House of Commons, and what steps have been taken to ensure that such an important thing as this shall not occur in the future.
In connection with the domestic issue, I was intrigued by the statement of the minister that Canadian Pacific Air Lines had been able to obtain planes and equipment which other air transport companies had not been able to procure. It was, I think, in connection with the routes in the Pacific northwest, and was obtained as a result of the fact that the company was collaborating with the United States in that field. What I am interested in in that connection-and it is merely incidental-is why the minister was so concerned about the fact that Canadian Pacific Air Lines were able to obtain these machines. Did the fact that they did so prevent the Trans-Canada Air Lines from obtaining them; and -if not, what possible complaint can he have in the fact that the company was so enterprising and energetic as to be able to obtain planes which could give service, and good service to this country?

speechtext: Does the minister wish to reply?

Yes. I might say that the item which the committee is discussing, and which I hope will be passed, is an item for the operation and maintenance of municipal airports, involving a sum of S39S.260. I can assure my hon. friend that he is making neither commitments nor entangling alliances at the present time. Much water must go over the dam before any agreements can be obtained. The government has put on record

its desires in the field of international aviation. I think no one would be more surprised than the government if its programme were accepted in toto by all the united nations which will wish to join in canying on civil aviation in the international field. Nevertheless the government has put its plan on record and for discussion before hon. members. We welcome discussion.
Then, I was asked whether an international agreement of the type discussed interfered with Canada's sovereignty of the air within Canada. The answer is that it would not' interfere in any way. No foreign aircraft could carry traffic between one point in Canada and another point in Canada. That comes under the principle of cabotage, and is expressly prohibited by the terms of the draft agreement. Then, flying between points in Canada and points in the United States is reserved for bilateral agreement. The reason is, as I said earlier, that such lines are merely extensions of domestic air lines, and it is felt that bringing such problems under an international board would be less satisfactory than direct dealing. I believe that answers the-questions the hon. member asked.

I asked whether the administration had considered, in view of the difficulties which would probably arise under an international agreement, the setting up of an empire agreement, so that we could get some kind of air route into effect, with a certain amount of expedition.

Expedition is not needed.
Air routes are being flown everywhere, as military operations.
I mean after the war.

After the war there will be
need for international air routes. So far as empire routes are concerned, no extended agreement will be required. I believe there will be no great difficuliy in flying from Canada to Great Britain, or from Great Britain to British possessions in the middle east, thence to Australia, and from Australia to Canada. It so happens it is not necessary to leave British territory to make that route, so that there could be no great problem involved. But all countries are concerned in a broader application of international aviation principles, in order that routes must not necessarily be confined within an empire family, or within empire possessions. That is the problem being disoussed here. If the problem were the simple one of travelling from one empire country to another, I do not think there would be any great need of discussion in the house. It would be quite simple.

But it would require some
planning, would it not?

What would be required? If
each country had a strong aviation service, with suitable aircraft, the rest would be quite simple.

It would be a question, for example, of what British aircraft would fly across the Atlantic, whether there would be a duplication of aircraft across Canada, which of them would fly from Canada to Australia, and so on. That is the sort of thing I have in mind, and I wanted to know whether that was deliberated upon.
That would be a very simple problem to work out.

Mr. Chairman, germane to the whole question of international civil aviation is the question of the propriety of a country like Canada delegating authority in this matter to an international body. That principle has been attacked and opposed in the house, and I regret that such attack has been made. I should like to state briefly our position which is in keeping with the principles of democratic government. Under that type of government we delegate certain authority to responsible bodies. In the provinces it is impossible for the population to get together and decide at a mass meeting as to what laws shall prevail. Therefore, the people of the province elect a government and delegate authority to that government. So long as the principle is maintained that in due course the government must go back to the people for endorsement or for replacement, you have a practical working out of the idea of democratic government.
We have the same thing in the federal field. It would be utterly impossible for Canada's
11,500,000	people to get together at a mass meeting in order to govern themselves. We want to govern ourselves, and accordingly during the process of time we have worked out a policy of electing certain citizens of the country as our representatives in parliament. We delegate to those people for the period of time that they are our representatives authority to direct the affairs of the people as a whole. There is nothing autocratic or dictatorial about that; it is just plain, ordinary common sense. It is democracy; it is being practical.
Some of ,us feel quite definitely that the time has come when that sort of thing should be extended to the world as a whole. I cannot help deploring-I hope I am a gentleman in doing so-the opposition there is to this idea on the ground that it is building up a dictatorship. When Tje attempt to carry this principle into world affairs we are trying to avoid having what I referred to last night, international anarchy. So long as the international council or authority which we set up and to which we delegate authority and power is responsible to the governments which have set it up, there will be nothing dictatorial or autocratic about it. That is what we must do if we want to make progress in this world which has literally become very small.
I wish to affirm again my pleasure that some steps are being taken, that some concrete accomplishments are emerging which indicate that it is possible for the peoples of the world, through their various governments, to get together to discuss the possibilities of

a government wider than a government on a national scale. I maintain that we should be practical when we discuss this kind of thing. There is no use in setting up bodies that merely meet together and talk. You must have an authority which will be able to carry out the wishes of the people they represent. That is why we in this group strongly supported the bill in connection with UNRRA; that is why we in this group were not hesitant to give our support to the government's attempt to throw into the pool of world thought some plan for the international control of international aviation.
I suppose, having said that, it would seem to add weight to the charges that have been hurled at the government from the left and right of us that they are trying to usurp the C.C.F. position in this matter. Therefore, I hope the minister will not impute any narrow provincial in-

terest to me when I ask a question, concerning the airport at Stevenson Field in the city of- Winnipeg. As the minister knows, Winnipeg is almost certain to be a very important point on the world air map of the future. The people of Winnipeg are conscious of that and are keenly interested in anything that relates to the development and enlargement of their airport at Stevenson Field, which is under the jurisdiction of the St. James-Winnipeg Airport Commission. If that airport is to serve the airways of the future as it can, and we feel it must, it will require considerable enlargement. I have had the privilege of seeing diagrams which indicate the kind of extension that might take place, calling for doubling the length of the present runways. If that is to be done, some thought will have to be given to the purchasing of property adjoining the field on the east end and the south, and some property on the west where buildings are located. I believe they are in fairly steady contact with the minister, and it would mean a good deal to the people of Manitoba if the minister would make a statement as to any plans which the government may have for enlarging the airport at Stevenson Field. I say again that I raise this question because I feel it to be of interest to the people not only of that area but of the whole country, because of the inevitable importance of Winnipeg on the air map of the future.

There is no question of the importance of Winnipeg on the air map of the present. It is the operating centre of the Trans-Canada Air Lines and the major overhaul base for Trans-Canada Air Lines. Stevenson Field is a very important airport. Trans-Canada planes going from coast to coast all stop there, and as far as I know it is adequate for any possible use that can be made of it. The largest planes that are flying stop there from time to time en route from the United States to Alaska. If at any time it becomes inadequate for the class of plane using it, I am sure that steps will be taken to enlarge the airport, but no steps are contemplated at present. The department has been asked to indicate how the field could best be enlarged when the time comes, and

a plan was drawn up indicating how the runways could be lengthened. That was done by the Department of Transport. There is no thought on the part of the government that any enlargement is now required. It is a first-class field in first-class condition, but if any time a larger field is required Stevenson's Field can and will be enlarged to meet such requirements.

May I remind the minister of two questions which were asked by the member for Saskatoon City which have not yet been answered. One was in connection with the so-called leak, to use a common term, with respect to the publication in another country of the convention which the minister put on the record here on March 17. Prior to that time, as the minister well knows, the question was raised, if not in the house most certainly in the press, as to why the convention which the minister tabled had previously been made public in the United States. There was quite a bit of speculation about that matter, and finally- the government placed the convention on the records of this house. I think the minister overlooked that question, which I think deserves an answer.
The other question asked by the hon. member was as to what report the minister can make with respect to what occurred at the conference held by the minister and Canadian officials with Mr. Berle of the United States which took place at Montreal.

As far as the leak goes, no one knows how that occurred. The draft convention was prepared in Canada, was studied by the war committee of the cabinet, and was forwarded to the dominions office in the United Kingdom as a matter of information. That was the only circulation it had at the time. But a copy of it evidently came into the hands of an -aviation, daily, published in the United States. I have no opinion whatever as to the route by which the document came into the hands of that publication.
In reply to the second question as to what happened in the conversations with Mr. Berle and Mr. Warner, naturally I was a party to the conversations, and I cannot divulge any more than was released in the press statement mutually -agreed upon. My hon. friend will understand that conversations of that kind are necessarily private, and that they were purely exploratory. We learned the views of the government of the United States; the government of the United States learned our views, and discussions were held in the direction of reconciling the views. That is all I can say.

That I presume was an
official conference between the officials of the civil aviation authorities in the United States and the civil aviation authorities here. I believe the minister said, in answer to a question of mine some time ago, that that conference between Berle and Warner and the minister and officials here was the counterpart of the conference held by Lord Beaverbrook with Berle during the last few weeks. I take it that this conference was the conference in which there was an exchange of views, an explanatory conference between Canada and the United States, and now there is the conference between Beaverbrook and Berle as representing Great Britain and the United States respectively. How can I possibly know
what Soviet Russia or Britain or the United States will doi in that direction? I can only say what Canada has done. I have no idea whether the others intend to publish their views or not.

May I ask the minister
this question, and it is important. The thing that concerned me when the publication was made was simply this-and I may be assuming 100-1431
too much. I wondered why Canada should be the first to make public what she is prepared to do. Yes. I am surprised at the attitude now being taken. The hon. member for Lake Centre was demanding the government's policy on aviation. Now great surprise is expressed that we did bring down government policy in detail.

There is nothing strange about it. Canada prepared a policy for civil aviation, prepared as nothing but a Canadian proposal. It was prepared with the knowledge of the views of certain other countries, but was wholly Canadian. Canada could do what it liked with its policy. It did, as a matter of fact, place it on the Hansard of the Canadian parliament. There may be two schools of thought on that. Was that a good thing to do, or was it a bad thing? There can be two opinions on that, but it has been done, and knowing the interest it has created in all countries which are interested in aviation, perhaps it was a good thing to do. That would be my opinion at the moment.

I should like to clear up this point with the minister. So far as getting the policy of Canada is concerned, I am quite certain that it was the proper thing for the government to enunciate its policy with respect to international civil aviation. We asked for it.
Yes.

We do not go back on that. All I am concerned about is this. Having done so, it seems to us that other nations perhaps might properly have done the sain., thing, to give us some idea of what they were proposing to do, as well as ourselves. I wibli to ask the minister this question, and perhaps he may not want to answer it. Was the leak in the United States, which in part put on

the public record what Canada was prepared to do, a factor in the publication of the policy of the government of Canada, or had the government the intention of making public to the nations of the world their policy first before other nations had agreed upon theirs?

Was there any discussion at any of these conferences with respect to other nations publishing what they are proposing to do in the international field?

The minister said that it was I who asked for the revelation of the government's policy in reference to aviation, and I have no apology for having taken that stand. What we have been endeavouring to do during the period the matter has been under discussion has been to ascertain what the government policy is; but in one or two matters, while we have received a considerable number of answers, many of them have been so equivocal as not to convey the information asked for. Before I ask certain other questions, in order to clear away a misapprehension created by two statements made by the minister, I should like to ask him the question whether the convention which was placed on Hansard on March 17 was prepared before the Beaverbrook conference or consultation or conversation, whatever is the proper description, or whether it was prepared after the consultations that took place among the nations of the empire.
I think that is hardly a fair question.
Well, Mr. Chairman-
What do you mean-was it typed before or typed after?
That is the usual way the minister has of answering. Was it prepared before the Beaverbrook conference?
Was it born?
Was it born, the hon. member for Yale says, or was it conceived in the conference and born afterwards? That is what we are trying to find out, because it is very important that the committee-
Suppose I say "yes" or "no." What difference does it make?
That is not what the minister is here for.
What is the hon. member here for?

The minister is here to give us information in regard to this problem. It is material to know whether this convention was a convention representing Canada's viewpoint as presented to the Beaverbrook conference, or whether it was a convention based on the understandings arrived at, generally speaking, at the conference. I ask him the categorical question.
I suggest to my hon. friend that he assume that it was, and that it was not, and then expound both situations and tell us where he arrives.

The minister's
attitude is not the attitude of a minister endeavouring to give information on events. That appears to be a continuing attitude shown by the minister toward members of this house and toward the country as a whole. I am asking him the categorical question as to whether or not the convention presented to the Beaverbrook conference is Canada's attitude? I am asking the minister that question, for at one time during this discussion he made one statement indicating that the convention represented Canada's view and was available at the Beaverbrook conference; and at another time he indicated that it was the consensus of the ideas of the various nations of the empire. Surely we have the right to know which is correct, or whether he was misunderstood. -I ask the minister, was that convention Canada's stand before the Beaverbrook conference, and was it presented there as Canada's stand?
In other words, you want to know the details of a private international conversation.
No.

One knows the
answer now, and the answer is that this convention was the stand that Canada took before the conference. I ask the minister to challenge that statement if it is not' true. I now ask the minister this question: was or was not Canada definitely opposed in this conference to an empire set-up?

My hon. friend is building up the greatest piece of nonsense that I have ever heard in my life. I suggest he stop questioning me, make his speech and sit down, because I am not answering questions of that type.

That is the attitude that the minister has repeatedly taken in this house toward questioners. He speaks of nonsense, grousers, yappers of the maritimes, et cetera. He endeavours to treat members of

parliament the way he might treat those who are under him in corporations. That is not the attitude that begets cooperation.

I am not looking for
cooperation.
It is perfectly reasonable to-
My hon. friend should understand that I am not looking for cooperation.

The minister says he is not looking for cooperation, but we are looking for information. The minister made a statement, and I am going to get answers to these questions which the people have a right to have answered. When I asked the minister this question in regard to an empire set-up last evening, he said:
Few countries would wish to be a minority shareholder in an international air line.
He did not directly say that an empire scheme had not been considered, nor would he say what the attitude of Canada was. This matter is one of the most important matters to come before this committee in so far as the future of the empire is concerned, and the people of Canada have a right to know what stand the government has taken with regard to this matter, binding as it will be on the people of Canada. We often hear it said in the House of Commons that there should be no reference to the empire, no flag-waving, as they call it. This is what Mr. Churchill said to-day in the British House of Commons amid cheers:
In a world of confusion and ruin the old flag flies.
Then he went on to point out the necessity for cooperation in this empire. One sometimes wonders whether we are arriving at a position in this country where it is not considered the proper thing to express pride in the empire and its future. To those I would answer that this is what Mr. Churchill said to-day in the British House of Commons:
Methods must be devised without haste to bring the nations of the British empire into intimate and secret council on world events not only during this war-because that is being done with great labour and efficiency-but after the war so that they will know fully our position and we know theirs in regard to the march of events and action which might have to come from them.
We ask a minister of the crown what stand the government of Canada takes in reference to an empire scheme, and the answer is one of contemptuous words. This is a serious matter, Mr. Chairman. We have endeavoured to place our viewpoint before the country and before the government-
Tell us your viewpoint in a very few words.

I asked a brief question and I did not get any answer. The question was perfectly pertinent. We endeavour to find out whether or not the government's attitude in this empire conference was one of cooperation after the war, and the answer we get is to the effect that-well, we are not going to be given an answer. We have a right to an unequivocal statement from the minister as to whether or not the matter of empire connections, future communications in the empire in a world-embracing air scheme were favoured or condemned by the representatives of the people of Canada at that conference. There must have been some discussion and yet we have no information on it. I find the following appearing in the Australia-New Zealand agreement of 1944:
In the event of failure to obtain a satisfactory international agreement to establish and govern the use of international air trunk routes the two governments will support a system of air trunk routes controlled and operated by governments of the British commonwealth of nations under government ownership.
I ask the minister, what did take place in this regard at the Beaverbrook conference? Did Canada take a position different from that of Australia and New Zealand, the United Kingdom and South Africa? Did she oppose a set-up within the empire, not excluding the international set-up, which will be necessary? Did she take the attitude she would not participate in a system of interempire trunk lines? These are matters upon which we as representatives of the people ol' Canada have a right to receive information. We cannot force the minister to give the information. All we can do is, as representatives of the people of Canada, to ask him whether one stand or the other was taken before that conference. The press reported that Canada was opposed in certain particulars to 'the stand taken by other dominions.
What press?
I referred to it last evening, and quoted it.
What press? A United States journalist, was it not, writing from Washington?	*
I referred to it in detail last evening, and the minister heard what I had to say.
Time magazine, was it not?

If the minister could just refrain from interruptions! If he has a question to ask I will answer him, if I can.

I was asking the hon. member what publication he was quoting from.
I gave the quotation last evening, and the authority, and there was no challenge from the minister.
Give it again.

The minister was present then and I have not it before me at the moment, but the reference is in Hansard, and no doubt the minister knows it. I ask him this: Did Australia and New Zealand and South Africa and the United Kingdom ask for consideration of an empire scheme? Did the minister representing Canada refuse to cooperate in such a scheme?
What did the press statement at the conference say? What did Lord Beaverbrook say?
Mr. Chairman, Lord Beaverbrook is not in this house. I am asking the minister in charge of the department.
I will give the hon. member the same answer as he gave me. My remarks are on Hansard. I once said that if my hon. friend would read more and talk less he would be much more accurate.

If the minister would refrain from statements which are so loose as to be equivocal, there would not be any difficulty in passing these estimates. I am asking the minister a question which he can answer unequivocally, and it will be accepted. But the people of Canada have a right to that answer; they have the right to know what attitude the government is taking in reference to this very important matter, which concerns the future of this empire; and I ask the minister to elucidate it, and give us an answer.

improper for any member of that conference to issue information' about the conference which has not been agreed to by the other members. I would expect my hon. friend to know that. If the hon. member

I do not wapt to take a lot of time. I spoke on this matter once last night. Some hon. members have spoken on it several times. But just for a minute or two I should like to ask a question or two with respect to some remarks which were made last evening.
Yesterday afternoon the hon. member for Vegreville spoke in terms of a loyal British subject, and with respect to the present international air agreement indicated that he was alarmed lest some of the sovereign rights of the people of Canada should be sold out to some international body. I followed last evening and pursued a similar line with some additional remarks. When the Minister of Munitions and Supply answered our speeches he said something to the effect that the foreign policy of our party was like the old Conservative British imperialism. I do not know exactly what he means by that. I am not posing as a profound student of political history, but I know that embodied in the British crown are the great principles of freedom, justice, righteousness and equity, and it is British policy that wherever the British flag flies those principles should be adhered to.
But never have.

I admit, of course, that
in the very weakened democracy and under the very weakened leadership of that democracy which we have had, a good many injustices have been done; nevertheless it is not the fault of those great principles for which the British empire stands. If by adhering to such principles as the love of freedom, justice, equity and righteousness we must be labelled
with a tag called "British imperialist," we cannot help it. I have sent for the dictionary- by the way, a dictionary is a good thing to consult once in a while-and I find that "imperialism" means the rule of an emperor. I do not think any one will doubt we have a king. Then there is the further definition: "Extension of British empire where trade requires protection of the flag." It is a great British tradition, that wherever the flag flies there must be liberty and freedom of mankind. I ask the minister if he believes that? If he does, then, according to the dictionary, he must be an imperialist.

He cannot be C.C.F.,
too.
M-r. HANSELL: The leader of the opposition may have something there. Then, with regard to "imperialist" the dictionary says, "Adhering to an emperor." I should like to know if the Minister of Munitions and Supply is adhering to the King of England, Great Britain and the Dominions beyond the seas?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The chair must rule
against bringing into the discussion in the House of Commons the name of the king or any member of the royal family.

I did not think the rule
applied to the mere mention of His Majesty. However, I do not need to go farther in that respect. I believe the minister is just as loyal to the crown as we are. I have no doubt about that, and I do not relish at all his flinging some term across the floor which is designed to discredit the Social Credit group, when we are only trying to be loyal to some of those great principles of British democracy. I shall not deal with that farther.
I cannot quite understand why there has been all the hurry in signing international agreements of this kind. It seems to me there must be some vying for position, while the world is in a turmoil. It would seem that somebody somewhere wants- to get in on the ground floor. There is a war going on, and we do not know when peace will come, although we hope it may come soon. But the invasion of Europe is not even started, and it is anybody's guess when the war will end. It is also anybody's guess what ldnd of peace table we shall have, or whether we shall have a peace table. Yet, while the war is in this state, nations gather together and begin signing agreements with regard to post-war air routes.
We do not know what the outcome of the war will be, in all its details. We know, of course, that we are going to win, because we vrill fight until we do win. But we do not know what the alignment of nations will
War Appropriation-Transport

be after the war is over. Italy is on our side only because she is in process of being conquered. There was a time when she was not with us. There was a time, too, when Russia had an agreement with Germany, and that was at a time when we were fighting Germany. The alignment of nations . has changed since then, and we do not know what changes will take place before ultimate peace comes to the earth. The whole picture may be changed.
Yet the Canadian government has to rush somewhere to bring about an agreement concerning which the people of Canada know very little. I do not wish to be too suspicious, but there is a feeling in Canada that there is something underlying these actions, and the way they are done. What difference would it have made, or what difference could it possibly make if this whole thing were deferred until peace comes, and the nations settle down to a better understanding? Would there be any harm in waiting until after the war? Would it alter our position at all?

There will be an awkward situation at the end of the war, if no international agreement is in effect. The air lines of various nations are flying over the world to-day in a manner which is suitable in a time of war, but which would involve great difficulties in peace time. For instance, British Overseas Airways maintain a military service flying around the world, over a great many countries. For that service Great Britain has no peacetime air convention. The United States flies to almost every section of the world. Canada operates a war-time service across the Atlantic, for which it has no peace-time franchise. To sort out these various services, so as not to cut off air communication entirely, requires an elaborate system of agreements. I believe it is highly desirable that, if possible, a comprehensive agreement be evolved before the end of the war, or before the termination of war-time aviation agreements.
For example, aircraft flying across Canada are operating under a permit for the duration ,of the war, and six months thereafter. At the end of that time Canada will be hard put to it to deal with the situation, unless agreements have been arrived at. There seems to be the suggestion that this draft agreement is ready for signing. I suggest that it is a long way from that stage. Preliminary negotiations are in progress, and I think one would be very optimistic indeed if he believed that these negotiations would not extend over several months. I feel we are not starting too soon to discuss this very important problem.
