I had really wished to ask the minister something respecting the future of present airports in the field of civil aviation. However, I have sat here for the past eight days and listened to this discussion, pro and con, and I have heard some members make almost the same speech on at least four different occasions. To-night I heard one man read into the record about forty minutes of talk that I have heard nine times since I came to this house-and it had very little bearing on the question before the committee.
When the hon. member for Macleod said last night that he was going to" talk on something he knew nothing about, I believe what he said might be applied to practically everyone I have heard discuss this question, including myself. I shall not attempt to discuss the matter in all its details. However, I agree with the position taken by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, when he states that if we are to achieve the objectives for which we are fighting, then there must be some international understanding with those people we term our allies in the fighting of the war. I agree with the position taken by the minister in trying to arrive at some understanding as to the future of aviation. Anyone reading the press, for the past eighteen months particularly, must be aware that those who have been in favoured positions for the last fifty years, those who have held imperialistic views and have controlled the cartels which have controlled production throughout the world, those who have controlled the machine which has strangled the world for the past fifty years, that small group in Great Britain and the United States, that powerful group which has had a monopoly of everything in the past have been endeavouring to achieve the same monopolistic position in regard to our airways.
I think the minister was well advised to have this tentative agreement drafted in such a way as to attempt to protect the rights of the people of Canada. I think this is the first step that has been taken in connection with any industry to protect the future of the people of this country. An effort has been made to protect this industry from those who were slowly but surely getting hold of it. The Canadian Pacific Railway were quite prepared to take over all airports and meteorological services. The complete development was carried on by the government with the taxpayers' money; the job of organization was done and the job of exploitation was about to begin.
The hon. member for Macleod and others have expressed their own opinions, but I think they are confused when they believe that the rights of the people of Canada are being given away under this agreement. For the

War Appropriation-Transport
first time our rights are being protected. I hope the time has passed when somebody in the United States or Great Britain can draft an agreement and bring it to Canada and have it accepted. I think this agreement is a step in the right direction. I am not going to say that I will agree with the minister or the government as to the manner in which this is to be put into operation. I am sceptical of some of the people who are behind the scenes or who will be in responsible positions when the organization is completed.
The hon. member for Lake Centre quoted a statement made by Mr. Churchill in the British House of Commons to the effect that in the midst of a confused world the flag still flies. The world is not so confused to-day. For the first time in some time the road ahead is beginning to look somewhat clear. Lines are being sharpened. World imperialism plunged us into the war, but the picture is becoming clearer. The peoples of the world who have been reading and thinking and hoping for a break in monopolistic imperialism see a much clearer picture to-day. We are not disagreeing with the fact that the flag stands for many great principles, but those principles have never been implemented. If this group is given the opportunity we intend to see that the principles for which the flag stands are fully implemented, something that has not been done, at least in my lifetime.
In spite of all the confusion that seems to exist about the action that is to be taken, may I say to the minister that I think he is on the right road. He should stick to his guns. I hope he will be realistic in the national picture when it comes to taking complete control of aviation in the future and will give due regard to seeing that the men and women who are to carry out the administration of this policy do it in the interests of the Canadian people.
I should like to ask a question about the use that will be made of our airports in the future. Many of these airports were established by small community groups and the local people have some equity in them. Many of these fields were taken over for military purposes, although I do not know whether they were bought outright or leased. They have been greatly extended and are in a position to do an important job in future aviation. I am wondering what will happen to the equity which these local groups had in the air fields prior to their being taken over. Will these local groups be compensated for the investment they have made?

The municipal air fields were leased to the Department of Transport for $1 a year, under an agreement which provides that the department would become responsible for
the operation of the airports, and for any capital expenditures required to fit them for war purposes. The ownership of the airports still rests with the municipalities. Such extensions as have been made will revert to the municipalities when the present arrangement is cancelled, unless some other disposal is decided upon by agreement. The ownership has never been disturbed. I presume the leases will be brought to an end and the properties again operated by the municipalities. There is always the possibility that by agreement with a number of municipalities a different policy may be adopted, but at the moment nothing has been done toward that end.

If I understand him aright,
the minister takes the position that since he was Canada's representative at a set of conversations in London last October, and since a press statement was issued at the end of those conversations, he cannot go behind that statement or amplify it. That would appear to me to be a perfectly tenable position. A statement was made in a responsible United States newspaper, which was referred to by the hon. member for Lake Centre, to the effect that Canada's position was said to have differed from that of England, New Zealand and Australia; that the mother country and those two dominions share a common view. Since that statement has been made we should like to know whether or not it is accurate. If the minister takes the view that because of the position he occupied he cannot go behind the . statement which was issued, that is a tenable position and we must be content with that.

May I say that the official statement of the conference as well as the statement made by Lord Beaverbrook in the House of Lords on behalf of the British government, would make it quite impossible that the statement referred to, which I understand is taken from a United States publication not greatly noted for being reliable-
Oh, yes; it is a Washington dispatch in the New York Times.

I thought the hon. member said it was from Time. Nevertheless the New York Times was not represented at the conference, and those who prepared the press statement, and Lord Beaverbrook, were there. ' Therefore I think my hon. friend would be well advised to accept the official statement and the statement of Lord Beaverbrook.

Would the minister place on some phrases that he used the same interpretation that I did? I listened to these sentences when the minister uttered them and

was not at all sure whether I got his meaning. At the bottom of page 2193 of Hansard of yesterday he said:
Canada is active in that direction. It must be recognized that no group of small countries can have any great influence on the final outcome. I think we must question the wisdom of attempting to group the small countries together as a bloc to go into a conference of that kind.
When he made that statement I wondered whether that to a considerable extent explained the position which the government takes with regard to the empire attitude. Is he there referring to small countries, Canada being one of them, the other commonwealth nations of the empire being others, including the United Kingdom, and does he question the value of those nations coming together for discussions in the hope of arriving at a common policy? Does he question the wisdom of that being done on the eve of a consideration and conversations which will be under-.aken by a far larger number than the nations of the commonwealth?

What does my hon. friend think? If he will read back a little he will find that I was referring to a suggestion that came from his left, that Canada should join with other small countries. That had nothing to do with the empire. My hon. friend, I am sure, cannot be serious in suggesting that I considered Britain a small country or Canada a small country. I assume that this is a serious discussion, and I think my hon. friend should ask serious questions.
My question was most serious. I listened to the minister with great attention yesterday.
I hope I have definitely cleared my hon. friend's mind on that point.
Right,

Were the possibilities of expansion into long runway airports taken into consideration when choosing the sites for the original airports in the commonwealth air training scheme when it was started in Canada?
'We thought of everything, yes.
Some of them will be rather queer long runways.

3. Civil aviation: Canadian government transatlantic air service, $400,000.

I would ask the minister with regard to the matter of the chosen instrument. He has told us in his statement that he and the government believe rMr. Stirling.]
in a chosen instrument to operate the international air lines, and I presume they will be founded on the basis of the present transAtlantic air lines. Is it the government's intention to have transoceanic air lines operated on a round-the-world basis or on a regional basis?
That is a difficult question. Would my hon. friend elucidate what he means by a round-the-world basis?

I mean a world basis. What is the basis of Canada's post-war international air service to be? Is it to be on a regional basis whereby Canada will operate air lines in only certain parts of the world, or is it to be on a world basis?

If my hon. friend wants a categorical answer to his question I shall have to ask him to elucidate a little more. What does he mean by an aeroplane operating on a round-the-world basis and one operating on a regional basis?

Well, Mr. Chairman, all I have to say is this, that the Canadian government has decided on a system of the chosen instrument and intends to operate international air services. My question is are these international air services to be operated on a regional basis?
Just what is a regional basis? Where do we go when on a regional basis?

Just a minute.
This is one question on which I am going to get a categorical answer. Are these international air services to be operated on a regional basis whereby certain areas will be allocated to Canada under international agreement, or does Canada intend to operate air services in all parts of the world on a transoceanic system? Under present conditions the situation in Great Britain is that she has a chosen instrument. Canada has taken a stand in favour of that policy. The United States has not a chosen instrument policy. The importance of this question arises in connection with the question whether we in Canada can operate international air services on a transoceanic basis, whether we have the necessary ability to do it unless we operate within an empire or some other international system.
I am endeavouring to ascertain from the minister what the plans are with respect to air transport on a world basis.

I may be overoptimistic, but I think Canada has the ability to do whatever any other country can do. We are operating across the Atlantic at the present time. I do not know whether that is on a regional or on a round-the-world basis. I am still

mystified by my hon. friend's terms. Would he say that across the Atlantic would be on a round-the-world or on a regional basis?

Facetiousness is
never an answer, even from a minister.
Really, I am not trying to be facetious. Regional is an odd expression. We expect to operate across the Atlantic and we hope to operate across other oceans.
Across the Pacific?

We hope to, yes, and we hope to operate into the south Atlantic. I do not know whether such operations would be round-the-world or regional. Perhaps my hon. friend would know. Perhaps he will be satisfied with that explanation.

I do not know whether the minister expects us to discuss the work of the department eo-mi-ally under this item
or to take each item as we come to it. I think it would be more satisfactory if we had a discussion of the work of the department as we usually have at this particular stage. It is unfortunate that the minister is not prepared to make a general statement regarding the work of his department. Can he tell us just what the organization of the department is, how it is organized as compared with other new departments? It is a war department. Last year we did not get a general statement nor did we have a general discussion, and I would appreciate it if we knew what this department comprises, what its functions are, and if we could get some general information about it before going into the items.
Mr. LaFLECHE: Yes, but I would repeat that I had thought of doing this year as was done last year. I may remind the committee that lengthy statements about the department were made in previous years. During the last fiscal year the department has grown to some extent, there being now nearly 300 more employees in it than in the previous year.

What is the total number of employees?
Mr. LaFLECHE: About 1,300. There are a number of departmental activities, and they are very well set out under the separate votes given in Hansard of February 11, 1944-War Charities Act, salvage, the civilian Canadian fire-fighters overseas, the committee on cooperation in Canadian citizenship, censorship with its subheadings, information and records branch, postal censorship, censorship of publications, telegraph and cable. There is an item here for the short-wave station of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation which is under construction at Sackville, New Brunswick. This is nothing new; it is merely to carry on.

When does the minister expect that to be finished?
Mr. LaFLECHE: I replied to a question in the house about a month ago. The officials of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation then told me that the buildings would be completed next month as a matter of fact, in May, and also that they hoped to be able to use the new short-wave station at Sackville late in this coming fall. There had been a delay, but it was an anticipated delay, the trouble being in getting the required equipment from the manufacturers. The delay itself was caused by the difficulty in getting favourable priorities over other war requirements. On that point I am quite satisfied that the officials of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation have done excellent work in going after priorities. There will still be a delay of

War Appropriation-War Services
perhaps four months over the opening date as originally anticipated, or as anticipated last year at least. I think they have cut that by two or even three months. Then there is the national film board, and we have the women's voluntary services, the government economies control, and the next-of-kin of prisoners of war branch of my department. I am only too happy to meet the pleasure of hon. members in attempting to give information, but I shall take the liberty of saying again that I think the best way to get information concerning my department is to take it up by sections such as represented in Hansard, pages 397 and 398, because we deal with such a large variety of matters between which there is no possible similarity.

I was going to ask the minister under which item the discussion will come in regard to educational services.
Mr. LaFLECHE: Under the next, auxiliary services. That is a large amount, $12,000,000.

On Monday, or when we take this up again, perhaps the minister will be prepared to tell us something about the auxiliary educational services. I believe that this is one of the best things being done in connection with our war services at the present time, and I should be glad if the minister could give the committee a detailed story of what is being done in regard to both prisoners of war and our own young men overseas. It would be a good thing for the country and the house to get a complete picture.
Mr. LaFLECHE: I shall be pleased to do so, and I thank the hon. member for suggesting it. I think there is a nice story to tell.
Progress reported.
